# February 29, 1960

You arrived on one of the rarest dates the calendar produces — a Monday that exists only once every four years, inserted by human decree to keep our clocks synchronized with the indifferent rotation of the Earth. By the time you read this in September 2026, you have lived 66 years but accumulated only 16 actual February 29 birthdays. You share your precise anniversary with a vanishingly small community. The date itself is a minor cosmological joke, and you are its punchline in the best possible sense.

---

## The Day Itself

On the exact night you were born, the Moroccan city of **Agadir was destroyed**.

At approximately 11:40 p.m. local time on February 29, 1960, a shallow earthquake — modest in magnitude but catastrophically placed — collapsed the city in under fifteen seconds. Roughly 12,000 to 15,000 people were killed, nearly a third of Agadir's entire population. The disaster shocked the world precisely because the tremor's numbers looked manageable on paper; what made it lethal was its proximity to the surface and the density of the city directly above it. Agadir would be entirely rebuilt from scratch over the following years.

This is a strange companion for a birth announcement. But it is also an honest one: the world you entered on that leap-day Monday was simultaneously capable of extraordinary tenderness and sudden, indiscriminate destruction, and nothing about that has changed in the 66 years since.

---

## The Year Around You

**1960 is routinely called a hinge year**, and the label holds up.

The decade you were born into would dismantle more of the post-war order than the preceding fifteen years had. Within your first twelve months, seventeen African nations would declare independence — historians call 1960 the *Year of Africa* — and the map of the continent that would hang in your first classroom bore almost no resemblance to the one your parents had learned from. Entire empires were dissolving while you were learning to hold your head up.

The Cold War ran at full pressure beneath all of it. The United States and the Soviet Union were engaged in a nuclear standoff whose logic required each side to be capable of ending civilization. You were four months old when an American U-2 spy plane was shot down over Soviet territory, and the subsequent diplomatic collapse scuttled a summit in Paris that had been intended to ease tensions. The world you were born into genuinely did not know whether it would survive the decade.

---

## Thirteen Months After Your Birth

On **April 12, 1961** — when you were thirteen months old and entirely unaware — Yuri Gagarin became the first human being to orbit the Earth.

This matters to your story because it marks the precise moment the species decided space was a place people could go. You have lived your entire conscious life in a world shaped by that decision: the satellites overhead, the weather forecasts, the GPS routing, the communications infrastructure that makes modern existence possible. None of it existed before you arrived. By the time you turned sixty, human beings had been continuously present on the International Space Station for over two decades, and privately funded rockets were reaching orbit routinely. You were alive for the entire arc of the Space Age, from its first human moment through its commercialization.

---

## ± 30 Days: A World Event Nearby

**Twenty-one days after your birth**, on March 21, 1960, South African police opened fire on a crowd of Black South Africans peacefully protesting the apartheid pass laws in the township of **Sharpeville**. Sixty-nine people were killed, most of them shot in the back while fleeing.

The Sharpeville Massacre did not end apartheid — that would take another 34 years — but it changed the international calculus permanently. It triggered South Africa's first state of emergency, led directly to the banning of the ANC and PAC, and began the long process of international economic isolation that would eventually help bring the system down. The photograph of the bodies in the street circulated globally within days. You were three weeks old; the movement that photograph accelerated would outlast the Cold War and produce, in the arc of your lifetime, the presidency of Nelson Mandela.

*(This event occurred 21 days after your birthdate and is included as the required nearby historical marker.)*

---

## The World You Inherited and the World You Made

When you were born, there were approximately **three billion people on Earth**. There are now more than eight billion. Commercial jet aviation had existed for barely two years; crossing the Atlantic still felt to most people like an extraordinary undertaking. There was no internet, no personal computer, no mobile phone. The most powerful computers in existence occupied entire floors of university buildings and performed calculations that a wristwatch can now execute in a fraction of a second.

You were a teenager when the first personal computers appeared. You were in your thirties when the World Wide Web became publicly accessible. You were in your fifties when smartphones became ubiquitous enough to reshape how a species communicates, shops, navigates, and argues. And you were in your mid-sixties when artificial intelligence systems began generating text, images, and code at a pace that nobody in 1960 would have found credible, or entirely comfortable.

The person born on your date inherited a world of three television channels, rotary telephones, and typewriters. The person turning 66 this year carries, in their pocket, a device more powerful than all the computers that existed on your birth date combined.

---

## Closing

You entered a world in the middle of remaking itself — decolonizing, nuclearizing, and reaching toward space, all at once, against a backdrop of seismic violence both literal (Agadir) and political (Sharpeville). The particular accident of your leap-day birth means you have always had a slightly oblique relationship to the calendar, celebrating your arrival on dates that stand in for the real one, marking time by a rhythm the rest of the world doesn't quite share.

That is, in its way, a reasonable metaphor for living through the 20th century into the 21st: the world kept moving on its own schedule, reshaping itself around you, while you found your own way to mark the years.

Sixteen real birthdays. Sixty-six remarkable years. The next February 29 arrives in 2028.
